units.title: Foundations for Functions
units.intro: A **relation** is a set of ordered pairs. Domain = all first components; range = all second. A **function** is a relation where each x has exactly one y. Vertical-line test on a graph: a vertical line hits the curve at most once.

cards.title: 1.1.1 Relations — pairing things up
body: In daily life we pair things all the time: a person with their age, a town with its zoba, a number with a bigger number. Mathematics records each pairing as an **ordered pair** $(x, y)$: the order matters, because "Hagos is the father of Selam" is not the same as "Selam is the father of Hagos".
**A relation** is any set of ordered pairs. We name relations with capital letters $R, S, T, \dots$
- The **domain** of a relation is the set of all **first** elements (the $x$-values, the inputs).
- The **range** of a relation is the set of all **second** elements (the $y$-values, the outputs).
Example: $R = \{(1, 2), (2, 3), (5, 6)\}$ has domain $\{1, 2, 5\}$ and range $\{2, 3, 6\}$. Read the first numbers for the domain, the second numbers for the range — never mix them.

A relation can also be described by a rule, for example $R = \{(x, y) : y = x + 1\}$, read "the set of all pairs $(x, y)$ such that $y = x + 1$". A pair belongs to $R$ exactly when it makes the rule true: $(5, 6)$ belongs because $6 = 5 + 1$; $(3, 5)$ does not because $5 \ne 3 + 1$.

cards.title: Worked example: from a rule to every form
cards.problem: Let $R = \{(x, y) : y = 2x - 1\}$ with domain $\{-2, -1, 0, 1, 2\}$. List $R$ as ordered pairs, give its range and say whether the graph is discrete or continuous.

steps.text: Put each domain value into the rule $y = 2x - 1$: $x = -2 \Rightarrow y = 2(-2) - 1 = -5$.
Range = the set of all second elements $= \{-5, -3, -1, 1, 3\}$.

The domain has only 5 separate numbers, so the graph is 5 separate dots: a **discrete** graph. (If the domain were all real numbers, the dots would join into an unbroken line: a **continuous** graph.)

cards.title: Discrete or continuous?
body: **Discrete**: the domain is a list of separate values, so the graph is separate dots — do not join them. **Continuous**: the domain is an interval or all real numbers, so the graph is an unbroken line or curve.

cards.title: 1.1.2 Functions — exactly one output for each input
body: **A function** is a special relation: every element of the domain is paired with **exactly one** element of the range.
How to test a relation given as ordered pairs:
- Look only at the **first** elements.
- If some first element appears twice with **different** second elements, the relation is **not** a function.
- If every first element appears once (or repeats with the same partner), it **is** a function.

In an arrow diagram: a relation is a function when **exactly one arrow leaves each element of the domain**. Two arrows leaving the same $x$ ⇒ not a function. Two arrows **arriving** at the same $y$ is allowed.

Example: $S = \{(-1, 0), (1, 2), (0, 3), (4, 2), (5, 0)\}$ is a function — the outputs 0 and 2 repeat, but no input repeats. $\{(13, 14), (16, 7), (13, 5), (18, 13)\}$ is not a function: the input 13 goes to both 14 and 5.

cards.title: Counting arrows that LEAVE each input
body: Left: every input sends out one arrow (outputs 0 and 2 receive two arrows — that is fine). Right: 13 sends out two arrows, so this relation is not a function.

cards.title: Relation or function? How the two ideas differ
head: Relation
Function

body: Every function is a relation, but not every relation is a function.

cards.title: Worked example: which relations are functions?

steps.text: $R$: first elements 3, 4, 6, 8 — all different. The repeated output 90 does not matter. $R$ **is a function**.
$T$: first elements 3, 4, 6, 3 — the input 3 appears with 4 and with 9. $T$ is **not** a function.
$W$: input 2 goes to 2 and $-2$; input 6 goes to 8 and $-8$. $W$ is **not** a function.

cards.title: Worked example: which value can x NOT take?
cards.problem: For $R = \{(8, 1), (3, 4), (6, 7), (x, 22)\}$ to be a function, which numbers can $x$ not be?

steps.text: A function cannot pair one input with two different outputs.
If $x = 8$, the input 8 would go to 1 and to 22 — not allowed. Same for $x = 3$ (4 and 22) and $x = 6$ (7 and 22).
Any other value of $x$ is a new input, which is fine.

cards.title: 1.1.3 Graphs of functions — the vertical line test
body: On a graph, two points with the same $x$-value lie on the same **vertical** line. So a graph shows a function exactly when no vertical line meets it twice.
**Vertical line test:** if some vertical line crosses the graph at more than one point, the relation is **not** a function. If every vertical line crosses it at most once, it **is** a function.
Reading domain and range from a graph:
- **Domain**: squash the graph flat onto the $x$-axis — the $x$-values it covers.
- **Range**: squash the graph flat onto the $y$-axis — the $y$-values it covers.
- An arrow at the end of a graph means it continues for ever in that direction; a filled dot is an end point that belongs to the graph; an open dot is an end point that does not.

cards.title: Sweep a vertical line across the graph
body: Left: wherever you place the dashed line it meets the parabola once, so $y = 3 - x^2$ is a function. Right: the line $x = 2$ meets the curve $x = y^2 - 1$ at $(2, \sqrt3)$ and $(2, -\sqrt3)$ — one input, two outputs — not a function.

cards.title: 1.1.4 Function notation f(x)
body: When an equation gives exactly one $y$ for each $x$, we say **$y$ is a function of $x$**. $x$ is the **independent variable** (you choose it); $y$ is the **dependent variable** (it depends on $x$).

To decide whether an equation gives $y$ as a function of $x$, **solve for $y$**: if you get one value of $y$ for each $x$ it is a function; if you get "$\pm$" (two values) it is not. Example: $y + x^2 = 1$ gives $y = 1 - x^2$ (one value) — a function. $y^2 - x^2 = 1$ gives $y = \pm\sqrt{1 + x^2}$ — when $x = 0$, $y = 1$ or $-1$ — not a function.

Functions are named with small letters $f, g, h$. Instead of $y = 4x + 3$ we write $f(x) = 4x + 3$, read "**f of x**". $f(1)$ means "the output when the input is 1": $f(1) = 4(1) + 3 = 7$, so the point $(1, 7)$ is on the graph. Note: $f(x)$ does **not** mean $f$ times $x$.
To evaluate $f(a)$: replace **every** $x$ in the formula by $a$ in brackets, then simplify. Brackets matter with negatives: if $g(x) = x^2 - 4$ then $g(-2) = (-2)^2 - 4 = 0$, not $-2^2 - 4 = -8$.

cards.title: A function is like a machine
body: Put an input $x$ in, the machine follows its rule, one output comes out. For $f(x) = \sqrt{4 - x}$: input 0 gives 2, input 3 gives 1, input $-5$ gives 3. Input 5 jams the machine ($\sqrt{-1}$ is not real), so 5 is not in the domain. The outputs are never negative, so the range is $y \ge 0$.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: What is the domain of the function $$g(x) = \sqrt{x - 4}$$?
cards.why:
**Step 1: Set the restriction under the radical**
For a square root function to yield real numbers, the expression under the radical must be non-negative.
$$x - 4 \ge 0$$

**Step 2: Solve the inequality**
Add $$4$$ to both sides of the inequality:
$$x \ge 4$$

**Step 3: Express in set builder notation**
The set of all real numbers $$x$$ such that $$x$$ is greater than or equal to $$4$$ is written as:
$$\{x \in \mathbb{R} : x \ge 4\}$$

**Step 4: Final Result**
The domain of the function is **$$\{x \in \mathbb{R} : x \ge 4\}$$**.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: Which of the following relations is a function?
cards.why:
**Step 1: Recall the definition of a function**
A relation is a function if and only if each element of the domain maps to exactly one element of the range. This means no two ordered pairs can have the same first coordinate.

**Step 2: Evaluate each option**
- For $$R$$: First elements are $$-1, -4, 1, 8$$. All are unique. This is a function.
- For $$S$$: First elements are $$13, 16, 13, 18$$. The input $$13$$ repeats with different outputs. Not a function.
- For $$T$$: First elements are $$3, 4, 6, 3$$. The input $$3$$ repeats. Not a function.
- For $$W$$: First elements are $$2, 2, 6, 6$$. The inputs $$2$$ and $$6$$ repeat. Not a function.

**Step 3: Final Result**
The correct relation representing a function is **$$R = \{(-1, 2), (-4, 51), (1, 2), (8, -51)\}$$**.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: What is the domain of the function $$h(x) = \frac{x}{x + 1}$$?
cards.why:
**Step 1: Identify denominator constraints**
For a rational function to be defined, the denominator cannot equal zero.
$$x + 1 \neq 0$$

**Step 2: Solve the inequality**
Subtract $$1$$ from both sides:
$$x \neq -1$$

**Step 3: Formulate domain in set notation**
The domain consists of all real numbers except $$-1$$:
$$\{x \in \mathbb{R} : x \neq -1\}$$

**Step 4: Final Result**
The domain of $$h(x)$$ is **$$\{x \in \mathbb{R} : x \neq -1\}$$**.

cards.title: 1.2.1 One-to-one functions
body: A function never sends one input to two outputs. A **one-to-one function** goes further: **no two different inputs share the same output**. Every output comes from exactly one input.

Test with ordered pairs: look at the **second** elements. If an output repeats (with different inputs), the function is **not** one-to-one. $f = \{(2, 1), (4, 5), (-2, -1), (6, 7), (8, 9), (3, 5)\}$ is not one-to-one, because 4 and 3 both go to 5.

**Horizontal line test:** if some horizontal line meets the graph of a function at more than one point, the function is **not** one-to-one. Points on one horizontal line have the same $y$ (output) but different $x$ (inputs).

Test with a formula: find two different inputs with equal outputs to show it is NOT one-to-one (e.g. $f(x) = x^2$: $f(2) = f(-2) = 4$). To show it IS one-to-one, start from $f(a) = f(b)$ and show this forces $a = b$.

cards.title: Sweep a horizontal line across the graph
body: Left: the line $y = 2.5$ meets $y = x^2$ twice (at $x = \pm\sqrt{2.5}$) — two inputs, one output — not one-to-one. Right: every horizontal line meets $y = \frac12 x^3$ once — one-to-one.

cards.title: Two line tests, two different questions
body: Vertical line test → "is this graph a function?" (one output for each input). Horizontal line test → "is this function one-to-one?" (one input for each output). Do the vertical test first; the horizontal test only makes sense for a function.

cards.title: Worked example: showing a function is NOT one-to-one
cards.problem: Is $f(x) = \frac{3}{x^2 + 1}$ one-to-one?

steps.text: Look for two different inputs with the same output. Because of $x^2$, try $x = 1$ and $x = -1$.
Two different inputs, same output ⇒ not one-to-one.

cards.title: Worked example: proving a function IS one-to-one
cards.problem: Show that $f(x) = 5x - \frac12$ is one-to-one.

steps.text: Suppose two inputs $a$ and $b$ give the same output: $f(a) = f(b)$.
Equal outputs force equal inputs, so no two different inputs share an output.

cards.answer: Yes — every linear function $f(x) = mx + b$ with $m \ne 0$ is one-to-one.

cards.title: 1.2.2 Inverse of a relation and of a function
body: The **inverse** of a relation $R$, written $R^{-1}$, is obtained by **swapping the two entries of every ordered pair**. If $R = \{(1, 3), (2, 5), (3, 7)\}$ then $R^{-1} = \{(3, 1), (5, 2), (7, 3)\}$.
Because the entries swap, the **domain of $R^{-1}$ is the range of $R$**, and the **range of $R^{-1}$ is the domain of $R$**.
The inverse of a function is **not always** a function. $g = \{(3, 6), (8, 6)\}$ gives $g^{-1} = \{(6, 3), (6, 8)\}$ — input 6 has two outputs. This happens exactly when $g$ is not one-to-one.
**Key fact:** the inverse of a function $f$ is a function **if and only if $f$ is one-to-one**. Then we write it $f^{-1}$ (read "f inverse"). Careful: $f^{-1}(x)$ does **not** mean $\frac{1}{f(x)}$.

cards.title: The inverse reverses every arrow
body: $f = \{(-1, 2), (-3, 1), (0, -2), (5, 6)\}$ is one-to-one, so reversing the arrows still leaves one arrow from each input: $f^{-1} = \{(2, -1), (1, -3), (-2, 0), (6, 5)\}$ is a function.

cards.title: Four steps to the formula of an inverse
body: **Step 1.** Replace $f(x)$ by $y$.
**Step 2.** Interchange $x$ and $y$.
**Step 3.** Solve the new equation for $y$.
**Step 4.** Replace $y$ by $f^{-1}(x)$ — and state its domain (= the range of $f$).
Check: $f(f^{-1}(x)) = x$ and $f^{-1}(f(x)) = x$. Quick number check: if $f(2) = 7$ then $f^{-1}(7)$ must be 2.

cards.title: Worked example: inverse of a linear function
cards.problem: Find $f^{-1}(x)$ for $f(x) = 3x - 6$.

cards.title: Worked example: inverse of a rational function
cards.problem: Find $g^{-1}(x)$ for $g(x) = \frac{x - 2}{x + 3}$.

steps.text: Collect the $y$ terms on one side: $xy - y = -3x - 2$.
Domain of $g^{-1}$: $x \ne 1$ (that is exactly the value $g$ never reaches).

cards.title: Worked example: inverse with a cube and with a square root
cards.problem: Find the inverses of (a) $h(x) = x^3 + 3$ and (b) $k(x) = \sqrt{x - 1}$.

steps.text: (a) $x = y^3 + 3 \Rightarrow y^3 = x - 3 \Rightarrow y = \sqrt[3]{x - 3}$. So $h^{-1}(x) = \sqrt[3]{x - 3}$ for all real $x$.
Square both sides: $x^2 = y - 1 \Rightarrow y = x^2 + 1$.
The domain of $k^{-1}$ is the range of $k$, so $k^{-1}(x) = x^2 + 1$ **for $x \ge 0$ only**.

steps.text: Inverse: swap, $x = \frac59(y - 32) \Rightarrow y - 32 = \frac95 x \Rightarrow C^{-1}(x) = \frac95 x + 32$.

cards.problem: Find the inverse of f(x) = (3x − 2)/5 and check it.

steps.text: Step 2: swap x and y: x = (3y − 2)/5.
Step 5: check with a number: f(4) = (12 − 2)/5 = 2 and f⁻¹(2) = (10 + 2)/3 = 4 ✔.

body: To find an inverse: replace f(x) with y, swap, solve, rename. Then check f(f⁻¹(x))=x on the new domain.

cards.title: 1.2.3 Graph of the inverse — a mirror in y = x
body: Swapping the coordinates of a point $(a, b)$ gives $(b, a)$. On squared paper with equal scales, $(b, a)$ is the **mirror image of $(a, b)$ in the line $y = x$** — fold the paper along $y = x$ and the two points land on each other.
So the **graph of $f^{-1}$ is the reflection of the graph of $f$ in the line $y = x$.** To draw it: plot a few points of $f$, swap their coordinates, plot those, and join them.
Points that lie on $y = x$ itself stay where they are, so $f$ and $f^{-1}$ meet on the line $y = x$ (if they meet at all).
Always use the **same scale on both axes**, otherwise the mirror picture is distorted.

cards.title: Swap the coordinates = reflect in y = x
body: $(3, 1) \leftrightarrow (1, 3)$, $(-2, 0) \leftrightarrow (0, -2)$, $(-1, 2) \leftrightarrow (2, -1)$. The dashed segment joining each pair is cut at right angles and in half by the line $y = x$.

cards.title: f(x) = 2x + 1 and its inverse
body: From $y = 2x + 1$: swap and solve, $x = 2y + 1 \Rightarrow f^{-1}(x) = \frac{x - 1}{2}$. The point $(1, 3)$ on $f$ becomes $(3, 1)$ on $f^{-1}$. Both lines cross $y = x$ at $(-1, -1)$. Slopes 2 and $\frac12$ are reciprocals — true for every linear function and its inverse.

cards.title: A curve and its inverse
body: $f(x) = x^2$ is not one-to-one on all real numbers, but if we keep only $x \ge 0$ it is. Its inverse is $f^{-1}(x) = \sqrt{x}$; $(2, 4)$ on $f$ matches $(4, 2)$ on $f^{-1}$.

units.title: Geometric Structure
units.intro:
Geometry here is an **axiomatic system**: undefined terms (point, line, plane), definitions, axioms/postulates you accept, then theorems you prove. A conjecture is a guess with reasons; a proof is a chain that forces the guess.

Attributes: sides, angles, parallel, perpendicular, convex, regular. Know the difference between a drawing (picture) and a figure defined by marks (tick equal sides, arrow parallel).

cards.title: 2.1 Axiomatic Systems
body: Awet and Kedija were asked to define a square.
Comment on two learners’ the discussion.
Awet: A square is a quadrilateral, where all its sides and angles are equal.
Awet: A line segment with endpoints A and B is the set of two points A and B and all points between the two points A and B.
A point is usually labelled with a capital letter.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: Which of the following represents the complete set of undefined terms in Euclidean geometry?
cards.why:
**Step 1: Define undefined terms**
In geometry, we cannot define every term without creating circular arguments. Therefore, we establish a starting baseline of terms that are accepted without formal definition.

**Step 2: Identify the baseline terms**
The three fundamental undefined terms that serve as the building blocks for all other geometric definitions are Point, Line, and Plane.

**Step 3: Evaluate other options**
Segments, angles, and polygons are all defined terms built from points, lines, and planes.

**Step 4: Final Result**
The complete set is **Point, Line, Plane**.

options.C: The sum of the interior angles of a triangle is $$180^{\circ}$$.
options.D: An exterior angle of a triangle is equal to the sum of its two remote interior angles.

cards.why:
**Step 1: Understand the definition of a Postulate**
A Postulate (or Axiom) is a statement that is accepted as true without proof, serving as a starting point for geometric reasoning.

**Step 2: Evaluate the options**
- "Through any two points there is exactly one line" is accepted as true without proof. It is Euclid's First Postulate.
- "Vertically opposite angles are equal" is a theorem that must be proven logically.
- "The sum of the interior angles of a triangle is $$180^{\circ}$$" is a theorem (proven using parallel lines).
- "An exterior angle..." is also a proven theorem.

**Step 3: Final Result**
The statement that is a postulate is **Through any two points there is exactly one line.**

**Step 1:** An axiomatic system starts from undefined terms, definitions and axioms.

**Step 2:** Axioms (postulates) are accepted without proof.

**Step 3:** Theorems are statements proved from the axioms; corollaries follow directly from theorems.

**Tip:** "Point", "line" and "plane" are undefined terms in Euclidean geometry.

cards.title: 2.2 Attributes of geometric figures
body: Geometric figures are described by their **attributes** (properties): number of sides, lengths of sides, sizes of angles, parallel sides, diagonals and symmetry. Knowing the attributes lets you classify a figure and reason about it.

**Basic figures:** a **segment** AB has two endpoints; a **ray** AB starts at A and goes on through B; a **line** goes on in both directions. **Collinear** points lie on one line; **coplanar** points lie in one plane. The **midpoint** of AB divides it into two equal parts.

**Angles:** acute (< 90°), right (= 90°), obtuse (between 90° and 180°), straight (180°), reflex (> 180°). **Complementary** angles add to 90°; **supplementary** angles add to 180°; **vertically opposite** angles are equal.
**Triangles** by sides: scalene (no equal sides), isosceles (two equal sides, base angles equal), equilateral (three equal sides, each angle 60°). By angles: acute, right, obtuse.

**Quadrilaterals:** parallelogram (both pairs of opposite sides parallel and equal, opposite angles equal, diagonals bisect each other); rectangle (parallelogram with right angles, equal diagonals); rhombus (parallelogram with all sides equal, diagonals perpendicular); square (rectangle and rhombus together); trapezium (exactly one pair of parallel sides); kite (two pairs of equal adjacent sides).

**Constructions with compass and straightedge:** to copy segment PQ, open the compass to the length PQ, put the point on a new point P′ and draw an arc; mark Q′ on a ray from P′ where the arc cuts it. P′Q′ = PQ. The same idea is used to bisect segments and angles.

cards.title: Worked example: using attributes
cards.problem: In parallelogram ABCD, ∠A = 3x + 10 and ∠B = 2x + 20. Find all four angles.

steps.text: Step 1: consecutive angles of a parallelogram are co-interior angles between parallel sides, so ∠A + ∠B = 180°.
Step 4: opposite angles are equal: ∠C = ∠A = 100°, ∠D = ∠B = 80°. Check: 100 + 80 + 100 + 80 = 360° ✔.

cards.why: A rectangle has equal diagonals; a rhombus has perpendicular diagonals; only the square (which is both a rectangle and a rhombus) always has both properties.

cards.why: x + 4x = 180°, so 5x = 180° and x = 36° (the other is 144°). 18° would be for complementary angles (sum 90°).

cards.why: The base angles are equal and the angles sum to 180°: 2b + 40° = 180°, so b = 70°.

cards.title: 2.3 Conjectures and counter-examples
body: A **conjecture** is a statement that you believe is true because of a pattern you observed, but that has not yet been proved. Making conjectures from examples is called **inductive reasoning**.

**Example of forming a conjecture:** draw two intersecting lines and measure the four angles. Whatever lines you draw, the opposite angles are equal. Conjecture: "vertically opposite angles are equal." It is later proved (each one plus the same adjacent angle makes 180°), so it becomes a theorem.
**Testing a conjecture:** try many different cases, including unusual ones (negative numbers, 0, 1, very large numbers, special shapes).

**Counter-example:** one example that makes a conjecture false. Conjecture: "the sum of two prime numbers is even." Counter-example: 2 + 3 = 5, which is odd. One counter-example is enough to disprove a conjecture, but no number of examples can prove it — a proof is needed.
**Number pattern example:** 1 = 1², 1 + 3 = 2², 1 + 3 + 5 = 3², 1 + 3 + 5 + 7 = 4². Conjecture: the sum of the first n odd numbers is n². (It is true and can be proved.)

cards.title: Proof habit
body: Given → diagram with marks → state a known fact (vertically opposite, alternate angles, SAS…) → conclude. One reason per line.

cards.title: More notes
body: You cannot prove an axiom; you use it. “Two points determine a line” is that kind of start. A counter-example kills a conjecture (one drawing is enough). Do not argue from an inaccurate sketch — mark what is given, not what “looks” equal.

cards.problem: Conjecture: "For every whole number n, n² + n + 41 is a prime number." Is it true?

steps.text: Step 1: test small values: n = 0 → 41, n = 1 → 43, n = 2 → 47 — all prime. The pattern looks convincing.
Step 2: try a clever value: n = 41 gives 41² + 41 + 41 = 41(41 + 1 + 1) = 41 × 43.
Step 3: 41 × 43 = 1763 has factors 41 and 43, so it is not prime.
Step 4: one counter-example disproves the conjecture.

cards.title: 2.4 Understanding mathematical proofs
body: **Deductive reasoning** draws a conclusion that must be true from statements already accepted (definitions, axioms/postulates, and previously proved theorems). A **proof** is a chain of such steps, each with a reason.

**Conditional statements:** "If p, then q" (p → q); p is the hypothesis, q the conclusion. The **converse** is q → p, the **inverse** is "not p → not q", the **contrapositive** is "not q → not p". A statement and its contrapositive are always both true or both false; the converse may be false. Example: "If an angle measures 30°, it is acute" is true, but its converse "If an angle is acute, it measures 30°" is false.
**Two-column proof:** list **statements** on the left and **reasons** on the right, starting with the given facts and ending with what was to be proved.

**Example — vertically opposite angles are equal.** Given: lines AB and CD meet at O. Prove: ∠AOC = ∠BOD. 1. ∠AOC + ∠COB = 180° (angles on a straight line AB). 2. ∠COB + ∠BOD = 180° (angles on a straight line CD). 3. ∠AOC + ∠COB = ∠COB + ∠BOD (both equal 180°). 4. ∠AOC = ∠BOD (subtract ∠COB from both sides). ∎
**Indirect proof (proof by contradiction):** assume the opposite of what you want to prove and show that this leads to something impossible.

cards.q: What is the converse of the statement: "If a triangle is isosceles, then two of its sides are equal"?

options.A: If two sides of a triangle are equal, then the triangle is isosceles.
options.B: If a triangle is not isosceles, then its sides are not equal.
options.C: If two sides of a triangle are not equal, then the triangle is not isosceles.
options.D: If a triangle is isosceles, then all of its sides are equal.

cards.why:
**Step 1: Understand how to form a converse**
A conditional statement is in the form "If $$P$$, then $$Q$$." Its converse is formed by interchanging the hypothesis ($$P$$) and the conclusion ($$Q$$), resulting in "If $$Q$$, then $$P$$."

**Step 2: Identify $$P$$ and $$Q$$**
- $$P$$ (Hypothesis): "a triangle is isosceles"
- $$Q$$ (Conclusion): "two of its sides are equal"

**Step 3: Swap $$P$$ and $$Q$$**
The converse is: "If two sides of a triangle are equal, then the triangle is isosceles."

**Step 4: Final Result**
The converse statement is **If two sides of a triangle are equal, then the triangle is isosceles.**

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: What is the sum of the interior angles of a 15-sided polygon?
cards.why:
**Step 1: Write down the interior angle sum formula**
The sum of the interior angles $$S$$ of an $$n$$-sided polygon is:
$$S = (n - 2) \times 180^{\circ}$$

**Step 2: Substitute $$n = 15$$ into the formula**
$$S = (15 - 2) \times 180^{\circ}$$
$$S = 13 \times 180^{\circ}$$

**Step 3: Perform the multiplication**
$$S = 2340^{\circ}$$

**Step 4: Final Result**
The sum of the interior angles is **$$2340^{\circ}$$**.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: Calculate the measure of each interior angle of a regular octagon.
cards.why:
**Step 1: Write down the formula for one interior angle**
For a regular polygon with $$n$$ sides, each interior angle is:
$$\text{Angle} = \frac{(n - 2) \times 180^{\circ}}{n}$$

**Step 2: Substitute $$n = 8$$ for an octagon**
$$\text{Angle} = \frac{(8 - 2) \times 180^{\circ}}{8}$$
$$\text{Angle} = \frac{6 \times 180^{\circ}}{8}$$
$$\text{Angle} = \frac{1080^{\circ}}{8}$$

**Step 3: Simplify the fraction**
$$\text{Angle} = 135^{\circ}$$

**Step 4: Final Result**
Each interior angle of a regular octagon is **$$135^{\circ}$$**.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: If the sum of the interior angles of a polygon is $$2160^{\circ}$$, how many sides does the polygon have?
cards.why:
**Step 1: Set up the equation using the sum formula**
$$(n - 2) \times 180^{\circ} = 2160^{\circ}$$

**Step 2: Solve for $$(n - 2)$$**
Divide both sides by $$180^{\circ}$$:
$$n - 2 = \frac{2160}{180}$$
$$n - 2 = 12$$

**Step 3: Solve for $$n$$**
$$n = 12 + 2$$
$$n = 14$$

**Step 4: Final Result**
The polygon has **$$14$$** sides.

cards.problem: O is the centre of a circle. A, B, C, D lie on the circle with ABCD a cyclic quadrilateral. The central angle on the minor arc AC is ∠AOC = 140°, B lies on the major arc and D on the minor arc. Find ∠ABC and ∠ADC.

steps.text: Step 1: the angle at the circumference on the same arc is half the central angle. If B is on the major arc, ∠ABC = ½ × 140° = 70°.
Step 2: ABCD is cyclic, so opposite angles are supplementary: ∠ADC = 180° − 70° = 110°.
Step 3: check: D is on the minor arc, and its angle uses the reflex central angle 360° − 140° = 220°, half of which is 110° ✔.

cards.title: Secants, Tangent and Chords: Properties
body: A **chord** joins two points of a circle; a **secant** is a line that cuts the circle at two points; a **tangent** touches it at exactly one point and is perpendicular to the radius there.
**Two chords intersecting inside** at E (chords AB and CD): AE × EB = CE × ED. Angle between them: ∠AEC = ½(arc AC + arc BD).
**Two secants from an outside point P** (PAB and PCD, with A and C nearer): PA × PB = PC × PD (outer part × whole secant).
**Tangent and secant from P** (tangent PT, secant PAB): PT² = PA × PB.
**Two tangents from P** are equal: PT₁ = PT₂.
**Example:** from P, a secant meets the circle at A and B with PA = 4 cm and AB = 5 cm, so PB = 9 cm. The tangent PT satisfies PT² = 4 × 9 = 36, so PT = 6 cm.

body: Plane figures have length and width and therefore they are called **two-dimensional figures**.
A solid object has length, width, and height.
**A solid** is an enclosed portion of space bounded by plane or curved surfaces.

cards.title: 4.1.2 Cylinders, Cones and Spheres
body: **A circular cone** is a solid whose base is a circle and whose lateral surface come to a point.

If a plane parallel to the base intersects a cone, not at the vertex, the part of the cone bounded by the base, the cross-section, and the portion of the lateral surface between the plane is called a **frustum of the cone**.
A sphere is formed by revolving a semicircle about its diameter as an axis.

cards.title: 4.1.3 Nets and Views of Solids
body: A **net** is a flat pattern that folds up into a solid. A cube has 6 square faces, so every net of a cube is made of 6 squares joined edge to edge — there are 11 different cube nets (for example a "cross" of 4 squares in a row with one square above and one below the second square). A regular tetrahedron has 4 equilateral-triangle faces; its common net is one large triangle divided into 4 smaller triangles.

Solids are also drawn by their **views**: the **front view**, **side view** and **top view (plan)**. A cylinder standing upright has a rectangle as front view and a circle as top view; a square pyramid has a triangle as front view and a square with its diagonals as top view.

The area $$A$$ of a regular hexagon with side length $$s$$ is given by:
$$A = \frac{3\sqrt{3}}{2}s^2$$

**Step 2: Substitute $$s = 4\text{ cm}$$**
$$A = \frac{3\sqrt{3}}{2}(4)^2$$
$$A = \frac{3\sqrt{3}}{2}(16)$$

**Step 3: Simplify the expression**
$$A = 3\sqrt{3} \times 8$$
$$A = 24\sqrt{3}\text{ cm}^2$$

**Step 4: Final Result**
The area of the regular hexagon is **$$24\sqrt{3}\text{ cm}^2$$**.

lessons.title: Surface Areas and Volumes of Solid Figures

cards.title: 5.3.1 Surface Areas and Volumes of Prisms
body: **Prism:** two congruent parallel bases joined by rectangular faces. Volume V = (area of base) × (height of the prism). Total surface area = 2 × (area of base) + (perimeter of base) × (height).

**Example — right triangular prism:** the bases are right-angled triangles with legs 3 cm and 4 cm (hypotenuse 5 cm), and the prism is 10 cm long. Base area = ½ × 3 × 4 = 6 cm². Volume = 6 × 10 = 60 cm³. Lateral area = (3 + 4 + 5) × 10 = 120 cm². Total surface area = 2 × 6 + 120 = 132 cm².

body: The ancient Greeks knew the formulas for surface area and volume of a sphere.

A ball in the form of a sphere has a diameter of 14 cm long.

cards.q: Find the volume of a sphere of radius $$3\text{ cm}$$.
cards.why:
**Step 1: Identify the formula for the volume of a sphere**
The volume $$V$$ of a sphere with radius $$r$$ is given by:
$$V = \frac{4}{3}\pi r^3$$

**Step 2: Substitute $$r = 3\text{ cm}$$**
$$V = \frac{4}{3}\pi (3)^3$$
$$V = \frac{4}{3}\pi (27)$$

**Step 3: Simplify the expression**
$$V = 4\pi \times 9$$
$$V = 36\pi\text{ cm}^3$$

**Step 4: Final Result**
The volume of the sphere is **$$36\pi\text{ cm}^3$$**.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: A right circular cylinder has a radius of $$7\text{ cm}$$ and a height of $$10\text{ cm}$$. Find its total surface area. (Take $$\pi = \frac{22}{7}$$)
cards.why:
**Step 1: Identify the formula for total surface area of a cylinder**
The total surface area $$SA$$ of a cylinder is:
$$SA = 2\pi rh + 2\pi r^2 = 2\pi r(h + r)$$

**Step 2: Substitute the given values**
Here, $$r = 7\text{ cm}$$, $$h = 10\text{ cm}$$, and $$\pi = \frac{22}{7}$$:
$$SA = 2 \times \frac{22}{7} \times 7 \times (10 + 7)$$

**Step 3: Simplify the expression**
$$SA = 24 \times \frac{22}{7} \times 7 \times 17$$
$$SA = 44 \times 17$$
$$SA = 748\text{ cm}^2$$

**Step 4: Final Result**
The total surface area of the cylinder is **$$748\text{ cm}^2$$**.
